report:
Your “no” is essentially right for **fracture prevention**: whole-body vibration (WBV) should not be considered an effective osteoporosis treatment to prevent fractures. The best evidence is indirect and inconsistent: trials/reviews focus on BMD, balance, muscle strength, or falls, while proven fracture reduction is lacking. A BMJ Open systematic review of RCTs in adults ≥50 explicitly looked for fracture/fall outcomes and did not establish fracture prevention: https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/7/12/e018342. The largest relevant RCT—710 postmenopausal women, 18 months of low-magnitude high-frequency vibration—was mainly about fall/fracture risk and did not provide convincing anti-fracture efficacy: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24676848/. A narrative review asking whether WBV could influence fracture risk in osteoporotic women likewise found the evidence insufficient/unclear: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6372741/.

Guideline framing matches this: the UK NOGG 2024 guideline notes WBV may reduce fall rate but **does not increase BMD**, and it is not a core osteoporosis pharmacotherapy: https://www.nogg.org.uk/sites/nogg/download/NOGG-Guideline-2024.pdf.

Bottom line: WBV might help some patients’ balance/fall risk as an adjunct, but for someone with osteoporosis the proven fracture-prevention measures remain risk assessment, vitamin D/calcium adequacy, weight-bearing/resistance exercise, fall prevention, and indicated anti-resorptive or anabolic medicines. Avoid high-intensity platforms without clinical advice, especially after vertebral fractures or with joint replacements/eye disease.
